questions.q: Define situational irony and give one example from the chapter where the narrator's expectation about school is contradicted by reality.
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when the outcome of a situation is the opposite of what was expected or intended. In the chapter, the narrator expects his father's death to free him for school (since his father had wanted him to study), but instead his mother pulls him out of school permanently to work — the very opposite of the father's wish and the narrator's hope. A wrong answer that cites "the narrator becoming a writer" as irony misses the point: that is a long-term outcome, not an immediate situational reversal. The error reveals confusion between irony and poetic justice or delayed fulfillment.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the school building functions as a symbol in this chapter, and what it represents beyond its physical structure.
questions.a: The school building symbolizes structured opportunity, legitimate knowledge, and a future the narrator is denied. It represents the institutional pathway to mobility that remains visible but inaccessible — like a door locked from the outside. A wrong answer that says "it represents education" is too vague; it fails to capture the tension between presence (the building exists) and absence (the narrator cannot enter). The error reveals a tendency to name the literal referent without analyzing the symbolic gap between access and denial.

questions.q: Identify a moment of dramatic irony in the interaction between the narrator and his mother regarding the father's wish for the narrator's education. Explain what the reader knows that the mother ignores.
questions.a: When the mother says, "The time that belonged to your father is gone; this is your brother's time," she dismisses the father's wish for the narrator to study. The reader knows (from the narrator's internal monologue) that the father's dying wish was explicitly for the narrator's education, and that the mother is twisting circumstances to justify child labor. The dramatic irony lies in the mother invoking the father's authority to do the opposite of what he wanted. A wrong answer that focuses only on the narrator's feelings misses the structural gap between the mother's claim and the reader's knowledge. This reveals confusion between dramatic irony (reader knows more than character) and subjective disappointment.

questions.q: Analyze how the label "vkuank" (orphan) functions as both a social stigma and a symbolic identity that the narrator eventually reclaims through writing. Support with two textual moments.
questions.a: The label "vkuank" is first imposed by the teacher Shri Lalasundar as a compassionate categorization ("vkuank" = orphan eligible for fee waiver), marking the narrator's vulnerability. Later, the narrator internalizes it — "I was an orphan in the class" — and it becomes a lens through which he sees his isolation. But when he begins writing, the same marginal identity becomes his unique voice: "I realized I could make poetry from my own father, my own mother, my own brother." The symbol transforms from a stamp of lack to a source of material. A wrong answer that treats "vkuank" only as a plot detail (fee waiver) misses its evolution from external label to internal creative engine. This reveals an inability to trace a symbol's dynamic arc across the narrative.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The mother's bangles are a stronger symbol of patriarchal constraint than the father's death." Defend or refute using textual evidence.
questions.a: Refute. The father's death is the structural rupture that removes the only advocate for the narrator's education; it is the event that makes the mother's constraint absolute. The bangles symbolize her traditional role and economic compulsion, but they are a symptom, not the cause. The text shows the mother saying, "If you had stayed in school two more days, you would have learned to write," revealing she knows the value of education but chooses survival. The father's death is the irreversible turning point; the bangles are the daily reminder. A wrong answer that equates the two symbols ignores causal hierarchy. This reveals a tendency to treat all symbols as equal in weight rather than analyzing their narrative function.

questions.q: Write a 4-line free-verse poem from the perspective of the stolen pen, using irony and symbolism to show its journey from a tool of the privileged to the narrator's weapon of expression.
questions.a:
I was born in a clerk's pocket, polished, proud —  
stolen by a boy with mud on his fingers,  
I wrote his father's name before he could speak it,  
now I sign the poems the school never taught him.  
A strong answer uses the pen as speaker (personification), contrasts its intended user (clerk) with actual user (mud-stained boy), and shows the ironic reversal: the pen meant for official records becomes the instrument of unofficial truth. A weak answer describes the pen physically without symbolic agency or ironic reversal. This reveals difficulty in synthesizing device and voice into original creative work.
